speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This was already an enormous undertaking and there were certainly hiccups along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nearly 200 FAST teams are now deployed and they have helped greatly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Among the safe distancing measures introduced, we had to stop communal cooking.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Officers then worked round the clock to ensure that meals suitable for the varied diets were delivered in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They coordinate schedules for workers to use toilets so as to prevent mixing, make sure the dormitories are kept clean and attend to workers' feedback and requests, such as getting paid and money remittances.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Workers from dormitories that had been gazetted as isolation areas were not moved as they would pose a higher risk of infecting others.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We then stopped further movements in and out of the dormitories to prevent cross-infections in both directions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the second phase, it was about getting the medical operations right.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The medical support plan was fully fleshed out, the infrastructure and personnel steadily built up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Regional Healthcare Systems deployed teams of doctors, nurses and technicians to each of the 43 large dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They tend to workers who are unwell, swab those who have shown acute respiratory symptoms, manage the cases that need to be sent to other facilities and assess if the workers are well enough to return to their rooms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They work with the FAST teams to set up on-site isolation facilities and organise safe conveyance from one location to another.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also set up four medical posts at the Tuas South, Kranji, Woodlands and Kaki Bukit migrant worker recreation centres to cover the larger factory-converted dormitories (FCDs) and construction temporary quarters (CTQs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For workers in the smaller FCDs and CTQs, we brought in the private healthcare groups as well as the nationwide network of Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPCs) and Polyclinics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If any worker was unwell, they got the same care as any Singaporean would.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The worker from Bangladesh who was transferred to a general ward after spending two months in ICU shows the extent of care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Furthermore, the cost of all tests and treatment is borne by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of Parliament like Mr Liang Eng Hwa are naturally keen to know if these measures are working.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The situation within the 43 large dormitories is largely stable now.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The picture among the thousand-plus factory-converted dormitories and construction temporary quarters is much more mixed and taking up much bandwidth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In many dormitories, there are active case-finding and swab exercises so that we can isolate and treat infected workers and break transmissions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of the workers are well and those tested positive are on the path to recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The full results of these efforts will, however, take time to show.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Outside of the dormitories, we identified another concern.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Infection among workers in the construction sector was noticeably higher than the general community and has not tapered off.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Supported by the health assessment of our MOH colleagues, MOM and BCA decided we needed to take further precaution and act quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We required all work permit holders and S Pass holders in the construction sector and their dependants to be placed on mandatory Stay-Home Notices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While they may not be infectious, it is safer to minimise their interactions with each other and the broader community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This involves building up community recovery facilities (CRFs) and housing recovered workers in suitable accommodation to minimise the risks of recurrent transmissions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must work out a way to allow recovered and uninfected workers to go back to work safely.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will again be an enormous challenge and not just the logistics of it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many workers will be re-housed and have to get used to new friends and habits, as Mis Cheng Li Hui alludes to.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many employers will have to adjust to their workers being in different locations with new arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will have to develop new strategies to monitor the health of the workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also have to plan for a more sustainable medical support operation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With telemedicine, we can still attend to unwell workers promptly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Task Force is focused on getting its job done.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is just mind-boggling when you think about it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For those on the ground, there are no ready-made solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many officers simply roll up their sleeves, work with the stakeholders to improvise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A Factory-Converted Dormitory (FCD) operator spoke to Hafiz and said he urgently needed to add extra toilets in a dormitory in order to effectively segregate the usage.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was near impossible to get new ones built anytime soon.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hafiz thought to himself what could be done and promptly sourced for suppliers of portable toilets, bringing much relief to the dorm operator and residents.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Task Force did not forget to bring some cheer to the dormitories when some of the workers marked their New Year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It worked with the Hindu Endowment Board and community groups to share sweet treats, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are now in the middle of Ramadan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the help of the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS), special arrangements were made for the Muslim workers to get their sahur, or pre-dawn meals, at 3 am, which means that the caterers also has to be preparing the food, well, around midnight and to get it delivered.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In every phase, the situation has demanded a scale and speed of response that is unprecedented.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The task force is keenly aware of its mission.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They know it is critical to get things right and to do it with heart.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will fulfil our commitment to the workers and pave the way for work and business to resume safely when conditions allow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Let us give the Task Force our full support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A bit of historical background is useful here.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the 1970s to early 1990s, most migrant workers in the construction industry came from Thailand and Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of them rented HDB flats or private residential properties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the early 1990s, many more construction workers came from China, Bangladesh, Myanmar and India.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To support their housing needs, the Government allocated land for companies to build self-contained dormitories with recreational amenities for their workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Building and Construction Authority (BCA), HDB and Jurong Town Corporation (JTC) tendered out these sites.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One important consideration was, "what would a migrant worker want at the end of the work day, if he cannot be with his family?" Well, it is to be with his friends, cook a meal that he would liked, practise his religious belief.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These dormitories were therefore designed for communal living.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To enable workers to live close to where they work and reduce the need to travel, the Government allowed some factories to convert part of their space for dormitory housing, subject to standards being met.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of these workers are from the Construction, Marine and Process sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have 20,000 workers housed in Construction Temporary Quarters (CTQs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another 85,000 Work Permit and S Pass holders from the Construction sector live in HDB flats, private residential properties and other premises.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Landlords must meet requirements and can be investigated for breaches.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government also set aside land to build recreation centres for migrant workers, where they can access supermarkets, remittance services and sports fields.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, there are eight recreation centres located in areas where there are more dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, we have taken steps to raise the housing standards of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A key milestone was the enactment of the Foreign Employee Dormitory Act (FEDA) in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The FEDA imposes higher standards on dormitories that accommodate 1,000 or more workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, licensed operators were required to provide common recreational facilities like TV rooms, gyms as well as provide access to amenities like mini-marts and WIFI in common areas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are also required to have health facilities like sickbays or isolation rooms and draw up contingency plans for quarantine arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM officers regularly inspect licensed dormitories to ensure compliance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, the Government reviewed these plans with the dormitory operators at the end of last year and conducted a table top exercise – what do you do if you have an outbreak?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But no one was quite thinking of something of the scale of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those were the rooms that Minister Lawrence Wong and I went to inspect.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, in dormitories with few infected workers, this provision has helped us to quickly isolate the close contacts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those who are infected, of course, are removed as soon as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But the close contacts, you can isolate them and keep them for a while.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked about smaller accommodation types.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Though not covered by the FEDA, they must still comply with a whole range of regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include BCA's standards for building structural safety, SCDF's Fire Safety Code and NEA's rules on sanitary facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To questions by Mr Png Eng Huat and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, regulatory agencies all conduct inspections.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There will be many more when other agencies are included.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Every year, MOM alone takes an average of 1,200 employers to task for unacceptable accommodation under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act and about 20 operators for breach of FEDA licence conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where lapses are found, dormitory operators must rectify them immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other than enforcement, MOM proactively engages workers, employers and dorm operators.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We conduct roadshows at the dormitories to hear from the workers themselves on improvements they would like to see.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: About nine in 10 say they are satisfied working in Singapore and would recommend their friends or family to come here.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Still, we educate the workers on what is acceptable accommodation and encourage them to alert MOM if they see something is not right.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, MOM started a "Colour my Dorm" programme about two years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A wall mural at Kian Teck dormitory was painted by youths as a gift to the residents.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Housing standards for our migrant workers have progressed over the years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is one of those that have been built since FEDA was passed into law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a slightly older one, but as Members can see, it resembles some of our earlier HDB housing estates.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When I visited Westlite Toh Guan, it really felt very much like that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This one has got ensuite facilities, meaning that company takes a room, the room comes with sleeping areas but also their own kitchen, their own toilet facilities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Next one, this what some of them look like inside.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It depends on the size of the room, how many can be allowed to be accommodated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is what a typical room looks like.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would say the size of the room, if you consider a badminton court, halve it and add maybe about 20% of circulation space, that is what you get.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The next one, one of the dormitories has got a supermarket which the migrant workers can use to buy the food they wish to cook.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The next slide shows – this is before safe distancing – what a gym might look like in the bigger dormitories.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will see how standards can be further raised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But, keep in mind that there are also older dormitories, which perhaps, have not quite reached these standards yet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What changes will be effective in reducing the transmission risks?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Will these changes require different space provisions and technical standards or stronger regulatory levers that Mr Louis Ng has asked about?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Inevitably, in any sort of environment where people gather in groups, there could be significant transmission.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the two places where there are substantial transmissions are homes and workplaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The virus respects no housing type, no nationality, no occupation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will therefore need to re-look how everyone interacts with one another at home and at our workplaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even the way we socialise will have to change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will need a focus on public education.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as Minister Lawrence Wong said earlier, we are still in the heat of battle.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We must be focused on bringing the outbreak under control and work out how we can exit from the circuit breaker and resume normal activities safely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When this is over, we will reflect and thoroughly look into areas where we could have done better, so that we will be better prepared the next time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Whether on the economic or health frontlines, it has been a real privilege to work with so many dedicated colleagues to tackle what our Prime Minister describes as "the challenge of this generation".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our tripartite partners have stepped up, and so have many employers and workers who are going out of their way to support one another.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many people take the time and trouble to send words of encouragement, including a hand-drawn card from a little girl, my resident in Bishan.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The MOM team has also been very moved by the many offers of support for our vulnerable workers, including our migrant workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC) set up the “Care Line” that operates 24/7.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The volunteers manning the line are migrant workers themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Among grassroots supports, Mdm Magdalene Poh from Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng sourced for and donated 10,000 bottles of hand sanitizers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ba'Alwie Mosque donated 450 boxes of dates to eight FCDs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To support the migrant workers’ emotional well-being, the sessions are conducted in the vernacular languages by volunteer counsellors, psychiatrists, social workers and interpreters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad now holds weekly engagements with these partners to coordinate efforts while protecting the health and safety of the volunteers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On such occasions, it is refreshing to hear what the migrant workers themselves say.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yes, it is hard to be cooped up in the rooms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yes, they miss their families and want to go home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But listen also to the voices from their hearts, an example of which is captured by the Facebook post of a certain Mr Mirza, who lives in a dormitory.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is what he had to say, “I on behalf of all Bangladeshi migrant workers in Singapore, want to thank the entire Singapore Government, Police, MOM, MOH and every security, every cleaner, every food supplier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They provide us food, daily needs items, mask, sanitizer, free WiFi/SIM card for our time spent in the room.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I am here today promising here in public if I got a chance to do something for Singapore, I will do it at any cost because they are doing their best for me.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will also do my best for them.” On behalf of all Singapore, I thank Mr Mirza for sharing his heartfelt acknowledgement and promise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Ministers for their very comprehensive updates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   To many Singaporeans, TCM is an important part of life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans rely on TCM to regulate their body.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Here, I would like to ask the Minister four questions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, we have both pharmacies and Chinese medical halls in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why the pharmacies are considered essential services and can remain open, whereas Chinese medical halls are not allowed to operate?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, authorities will allow shops selling ice cream, cakes and desserts to resume operation from 12 May, but other Chinese medical halls are still not allowed to open.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it because Chinese medicine is not as tasty as ice creams and cakes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The last question, under what circumstances will Government allow all Chinese medical halls to resume operation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many neighbourhood medical halls do not have a resident TCM practitioner.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A lot of residents find it very inconvenient if the medical halls remain closed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I mentioned in my Statement, we are beginning to allow some of the business activities to resume and for life to begin to return to normal, but we need to do so in a very careful way, in a very calibrated way, step by step, while in the meantime putting in precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, the overriding priority is still to encourage Singaporeans to stay at home as much as possible, go out only when necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And similarly even for business activities, including TCM practices, we would also want to make sure that we open it in a safe way to minimise the risk of further transmission and further infection.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Particularly in medical practices, including TCM practices, there is a lot of close personal contact and interactions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we want to be particularly careful with this, and therefore, the answer is not totally "no", but we need to watch very carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And if we are able to continue to keep the infection numbers low and are able to put in place additional precautionary measures, we will progressively open many of these services and facilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have one question for Minister Josephine and four questions for Minister Gan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first question is to Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is with regard to MOM's efforts on the economic front, the first half of her statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The key objective of the JSS was to encourage companies to retain workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, some employers are indicating that the COVID-19 circuit breaker measures have made their businesses are no longer viable and retrenchments for Singapore workers are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There has also been some evidence of residents coming up to us and saying employers have instituted wage cuts, no pay leave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry have any estimate of the retrenchment numbers it is anticipating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And is the Government planning additional support measures, particularly for the low- and middle income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first pertains to COVID-19 testing for foreign workers, which number up to 1.1 million in Singapore as of December 2019, excluding foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government have a roadmap to potentially test all the foreign workers progressively, starting with construction workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The third question pertains to the impediments to widespread testing early on in early April when the task force said that about 1,500 to 2,500 tests were conducted daily.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This number is potentially to be scaled up to 40,000, as the Minister just shared.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share what were the impediments and how these impediments were overcome to reach this number?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And by when can we expect 40,000 tests to be conducted on a daily basis?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By when does the task force expect all commercial establishments to institute or to ensure that the SafeEntry app is used before Singaporeans can enter the those premises?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the time being, we have an added challenge which is that data collection during this period is not as easy as it was.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Surveys that are sent to companies may not be picked up in time, because some companies work from home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, if we have their emails, we will send it to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some companies expressed their difficulties to us, for example, in accessing their own databases in order to provide information to MOM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we have some of these challenges to overcome.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nonetheless, I think there is not much point and value in us speculating what the retrenchment and unemployment numbers will be like.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the key is working with the tripartite partners to plan for recovery of economic activities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier in the Ministerial Statement that Minister Lawrence Wong made, he talked about very important changes that we need to make at workplaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One thing he said – I am not not sure if Members picked up – was the idea of safe management.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Meaning, depending on the workplace situation, how do you ensure that workers can continue to come to work and remain safe.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we are focusing all of our efforts on that front.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: By now, the number would have grown to close to 30,000 foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Do we have a plan to test all foreign workers?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our testing is still very targeted for specific purposes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do testing on dormitories generally to establish the baseline level of infection in each dormitory so that we are able to strategise how we respond to the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And we also do baseline testing of workers in general to have a sense of where we are in terms of the infection rates.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But for those who are infected in selected dormitories, we also do aggressive testing in order to allow us to identify infected workers so that we can isolate them and to protect those who are not infected.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, these are strategies that we have put in place for the management of a dormitory and the testing will be aligned with the strategy in managing these dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we are also looking at testing more of the essential workers that are going to continue to work in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These would include the foreign workers as well as Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For the foreign workers who are continuing to work in the essential industries, we will have to test them, not just once but repeatedly because they would continue to be exposed in the community and at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, there may be a need to repeat the test on them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These essential workers, the number will grow as we begin to restore more of the business activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, it is important for us to do so in a safe way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Testing, as I mentioned, is an important part of the strategy to ensure the safe opening and the safe restoration of some of the business activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will need to look at how we can source for more test kits, both manufacturing locally as well as through procuring internationally to allow us to have more capacity to do testing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we are also looking at materials because each test will also require materials for the testing, such as the reagents that will be needed for the extraction of the RNA materials.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is not enough to just ensure that we have the test kit, but we also need to have the RNA extracted and therefore, we have to make sure that we have sufficient supplies of these materials.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And thirdly, there are manpower requirements because we can do the swabs but having swabbed the individuals, we still need to process the swabs, document them, test them and have the results properly recorded.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I would not be able to promise you when but we are doing our best to ramp it up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we also have to be mindful that, in fact, there is a global shortage of some of these test kits and the reagents.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, we have to ensure that we have a continued supply and stock of these materials to allow us to continue and sustain this high level of testing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One is related to the personal protective equipment (PPE) that our medical staff use.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can I ask if we still have sufficient supply in Singapore and stockpile?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some other HBB residents have written in to me asking if there was a reason why they, who do not run F&B HBBs but take similar precautions in dealing with delivery men, are not similarly allowed to continue, if the risk for both groups are the same.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We should always try to preserve our PPE because this is going to be a long fight and whatever stockpile that we have, we will continue to need to require the supply chain to be preserved so that we are able to continue to import more of the equipment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We continue to need masks and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think we will have to continue to remain vigilant to conserve our supplies and the key strategy is really to keep the number of cases low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But beyond that, other kinds of retail, whether it is a physical retail outlet or a home-based retail, we are still at this stage not allowing but as we said, we continue to monitor the situation closely and we will see whether the conditions permit for further easing of the measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I ask the Minister what is MOH's position on this new treatment and if MOH is reviewing this as a potential treatment for our patients?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second question is for the Manpower Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is not the only country that has migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many countries have a large number of migrant workers to complement their manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also concurrently discussing with pharmaceutical companies to see whether we are able to have access to additional allocation over and above what is allocated for the trial.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   There are about 10 million migrant workers who leave their hometown and come to Southeast Asia to work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Only a small portion of them come to Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are a lot more of them working in Malaysia and Thailand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Countries have their own ways of dealing with the COVID-19 outbreak, including how they want to handle the health issue of their migrant workers and other migrant worker related matters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We need not to speculate whether the infection rate among migrant workers in other countries is higher or lower than Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What we can say is that, each country will have its own considerations and constraints, especially when it comes to testing and treatment which may not be the same as Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our stance is to tackle this issue comprehensively, including setting out clear strategies and providing sufficient resources, and very importantly, ensuring a tight organisation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of course, with the COVID-19 situation, migrant workers not only worry about health, but also their livelihood.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Quite often, their hometown was also under lockdown or affected by different measures, therefore their family’s livelihood is also under threat.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, when we deal with the migrant workers related issues, besides ensuring that their meals are taken care of, we also look after their other needs, such as getting wages and remitting money back to their hometown.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our comprehensive approach ensures their health as well as their needs in daily life are being taken care of.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we continue to go in this direction, even if some migrant workers are infected, the symptoms are very mild.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should focus all our energy on helping them recover.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I have a question for the Minister for Health and then two questions for the other Ministers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To Minister Gan, I understand that there is a lot of concern regarding the mental well-being and mental health of the migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to the factory-converted dormitories, which clearly are more dispersed, teleconsultation is being used to support the physical health needs of the migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The other two questions, the first which I actually highlighted in my Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We know that the experts are saying it is not a "if", it is a "when".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is especially so given that the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act (FEDA) provides very explicitly for quarantine preparation and testing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we have learned that that legislative provision may or may not be enough.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The third is to all the Ministers and also, since the Prime Minister is here, is will the Government consider issuing an apology to the migrant workers, given the dismal conditions that they are currently in, because of the conditions of dormitories and all the other conditions, and especially now that they are in complete lockdown for the sake and safety of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Allow me to address the issue on mental health and then I will leave the other two Ministers to address the other two questions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Indeed, mental health is a part of a very important consideration in our healthcare system and particularly on the ground, with regard to dealing with our foreign workers who are in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our medical teams on the ground are linked back to the various Regional Healthcare Systems.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Within these Regional Healthcare Systems, they have support from the entire healthcare system, including mental health as well as other healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They have a full range of services available to them and they will assess the situation on the ground and decide in what form the mental health support is needed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They will also be dealing with the individual cases, assessing each individual patient.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even those who are non-patients, those who are not infected with COVID-19, could also have mental health issues and we are quite mindful of their mental health needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The medical team on the ground is paying attention to the mental health conditions of the workers in the dormitories, as well as those outside the dormitories, where these medical teams are involved in.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Beyond the medical teams, we also have a FAST team, as Minister Josephine Teo highlighted.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Within this team, they are also very mindful of paying attention to the well-being of the foreign workers in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These include not just their meals, their hygiene and their daily activities, but also their mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The inter-agency task force looking after these dormitory operations is very mindful of the mental health needs, is paying attention to this and is working with the medical team on the ground with strong support from the various Regional Healthcare Systems to provide mental health services to those workers who may need them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is more than just a review on dormitories.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a review on the whole pandemic from start to finish and our response, and we are committed to learning and improving from this experience.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what I said, so let there be no doubt that we are not wanting to do this because after the crisis is over, we will do a full review.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The actual nature of it, the form of it, the timing of it – clearly, it is not possible to say it today when we are still fighting a battle for which we do not know when it will end.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But after that, we are committed to doing a review, and we will announce it as and when we are ready.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We interact very closely with the workers themselves on a very regular basis at the dormitories and even outside the dormitories, whenever our FAST teams follow up on their requests and feedback.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that what they are focused on is how we can help them to handle this present situation – not fall sick and if they fall sick, how to take care of them, how to ensure their wages are being paid, how to ensure that they can send money home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think they are doing a lot to help with the food, the sanitation, the healthcare, but I hope that Minister Josephine can also look into the gross floor area that I raised in my Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is very hard for some of the workers to practise safe distancing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we have a second wave of infections and the workers go back to this 4.5 sqm, then I think that we will get large clusters in our dormitories again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could I ask Minister Josephine if we can review this urgently?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some individuals who are in the Community Isolation Facilities (CIFs), they are clinically well but they continue to be tested positive in repeated tests.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And some of them have been in the CIFs for more than a month.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Understandably, they themselves or even their family members are anxious.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What more can be done medically to assist their discharge, especially those who are asymptomatic?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The second supplementary question is for Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How does MOM keep track of the residential locations of all the work permit holders or the S Pass holders?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Will contact tracing still be required in future on the group of foreign workers who are in the essential services due to their proximity at their workplace and also their social culture?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can we better implement the tracing of these workers and ringfence any possible issues that may arise from the workers who are living outside the dormitories?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Indeed, we do find many patients in our CCFs as well as in our hospitals and in our isolation centres who continue to test positive.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The theory is that many of these tests may be picking up fragments of the virus and some of these viruses may no longer be viable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But nonetheless, the test will be able to pick them up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: After 21 days, it is even more difficult to culture these viruses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, in effect, many of the scientists have come to the conclusion that probably, the RNA that has been detected are fragments of the virus and they are no longer viable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So far, we have been keeping them in the Community Care Facilities (CCFs).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Member is right that to keep them in the CCF is also not very good for them because they are not able to move around freely.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are exploring with our infectious disease experts to see what else can we do beyond just testing them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For some of them, you may still test positive after months because they just continue to have these fragments which may not be viable anymore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we may need to think about what we can do to help them so that they can be discharged, go home and go back to normal life if they are no longer infectious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will have to look into better ways of encouraging the workers and their employers to update this database.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If necessary, we may have to put in place stronger measures to make this happen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because, as this episode shows, it is quite important for us to be able to know their exact whereabouts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Miss Chan says, in future, for contact tracing purposes, it is not just their residential addresses, it may have to be some other means as well.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My question is for Minister Gan Kim Yong.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is reported in many countries, including the US and the UK, that due to fear of the virus, even people with serious health emergencies such as heart attacks or strokes are not going to the hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Indeed, it is important for Singaporeans to understand that if you have a serious medical condition, do go and see a doctor or do call the ambulance so that they can send you to an emergency department to be attended to.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think it is important for us to encourage Singaporeans to seek medical attention whenever necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: From the hospitals' point of view, even though we have deferred some of the more stable patients' appointments, we do continue to keep in touch with them, including through teleconsult, to make sure that they remain all right and stable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For these patients, we are keeping a close watch and if it is necessary, the hospital will call them back for treatment and for surgery, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to continue to monitor these patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to educate them on the signs of critical illness and when they ought to seek medical attention.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I have two supplementary questions for Minister Gan.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I am very glad to note that MOH is providing mental well-being support for our frontline workers, especially doctors and nurses who face patients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Like frontliners, they also face heavy workloads, physical and mental stress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The second one is, if mental well-being support is provided, what is the type of support that is being done for them?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All these are part and parcel of the mental health support that we are giving to our healthcare workers, both on the professional side as well as the support staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we do for all staff who are on the frontline.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apparently, this is something that is being looked at in Switzerland and Australia and is a way to determine where there could possibly be clusters of infection in a particular building or particular locality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is that something that we will be looking at going forward?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As far as I understand, currently people with acute respiratory symptoms, not all of them currently are being tested for COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure if my understanding is correct.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is that something that the Ministry is looking to review?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, right now, when you have close contacts of a confirmed COVID-19 case in the community, some are given Stay-at-Home Notices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think Minister Gan talked about vaccines in his speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The developments in this space seem to be moving very rapidly and there is news coming from different teams around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are plans being made to push that out, roll that out to the population and prioritisation being given to seniors and so on?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My last question is for Minister Lawrence Wong and it is on HDB commercial leases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is feedback from some micro businesses and SMEs about the rules for re-assignment of HDB commercial leases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a logic to those rules, not to allow re-assignment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But would HDB consider allowing a micro business – rather than having to break the lease, give notice, vacate and reinstate the premises, which is time-consuming and costly – to re-assign to another business that might want to take it up, just as a short-term measure during this crisis period?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But there are challenges because sewage, by nature, would have been significantly diluted because it is a collection of quite a large population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we will need to test the sensitivity and see whether we are able to pick up sufficient fragments to be able to determine whether there is significant infection in the particular target areas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that we are studying but it has its inherent challenges and we may not be able to deploy it for all kinds of settings.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But in the high concentration settings, that may be possible.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But, then, if there is a high concentration of infected cases, you probably would have detected these cases in any case.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is something that we are continuing to study and see whether we could deploy them in a meaningful way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also looking at whether we can expand beyond just PARI to see whether we can enhance or increase the number of tests that we do on the ARIs, that is, those with acute respiratory illnesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we also have to bear in mind that we have to assess whether it is productive and going to be effective because the number of cases that would turn positive from the ARIs may be quite low and, therefore, you may end up testing a lot, but not being able to pick up a very meaningful number of cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But having said that, we do have, as I have mentioned earlier, a surveillance system where we sample ARI patients and those with flu-like symptoms to have a sense of what is the prevalence level in the population, in the community, to assess whether there is widespread community transmission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I have mentioned earlier, it does not seem to be so at this moment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For the confirmed cases and those who are in quarantine, whether we will test all of them, so far, our testing for the persons under quarantine is on a very selective basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I have mentioned in my speech as well, we do a risk assessment for those who have very close contacts and including the children who are not able to explain whether they feel ill or not.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, those we will quite aggressively test them to make sure that they are not infected.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And for the rest of those quarantined, it will also depend on the risk assessment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And as we have more capacity, we hope to be able to test more of them to minimise the risk of transmission.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think there are a lot of news media reports about the progress made.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to do what we need to do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we hope that the vaccine will come soonest possible and we are involved in some of the collaborative research work internationally.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we are tapped into the progress and we hope that the vaccines will come out soon.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I think it will still take some time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is better for us to now focus on the immediate tasks that we need to address.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, restrictions were put in place for a good reason.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will consider whether some flexibility might be extended during this time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think we should not lose sight of the underlying objectives and rationale for why some of these measures were put in place to begin with.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think, again, we should look at it in a broader context.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are many measures that have been put in place to help businesses, including rental rebates and measures that MOF has announced through three successive Budgets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us look at this holistically to see what is the best way to help our businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have three supplementary questions for Minister Gan on the testing of migrant workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has explained that earlier in the statement, I think.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, my first question is, how are we managing then the risk resulting from the fact that some of the younger workers may not be tested, detected and isolated for now while we still have these resource constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And I am referring here to the risk within dormitories, not so much the wider community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, have we been communicating the reasons for these testing strategies to migrant workers and Singaporeans sufficiently?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Again, the migrant workers may not be aware of why some of these strategies are being carried out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, are the strategies for testing aligned between the different dormitories?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Then we have been hearing some reports that the strategies may differ, depending on who is in charge on the ground and various other operational considerations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Whether or not they are COVID-19, we will take them out so that we pay particular attention in attending to their medical needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But for the foreign workers who remain in the dormitories, the priority is to make sure that their well-being is taken care of, provide them with the medical attention without having to wait for the test results.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And within the dormitories, there are isolation facilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Where possible, we put them in the isolation facilities where some of them may be cohorted together because they all have similar illnesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For the different dormitories, we align them in terms of our strategy or approach.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is coordinated again by the inter-agency task force that is managing the dormitories and they have a comprehensive framework of how to manage each dormitory.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are some bigger ones and there are some smaller ones, and there are dormitories which have a higher level of infection and there dormitories which have relatively low level of infection.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The approach would have to be quite different, depending on the nature of the infection within these dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the key priority is to make sure that all infected patients, all ill patients are taken care of.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are also patients who report sick which are not related to COVID-19 and not related to infection, and we continue to take care of them and to treat them where necessary and appropriate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And there are cases where they need hospital attention which are not related to COVID-19, we also will have to send them to hospital for medical attention.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, the key is to ensure that each worker in the dormitory is taken care of.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When they have medical needs, we must respond to their medical requirements to make sure that they are taken care of and, at the same time, do what we can to minimise fatalities among our COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I understand, the efficacy level is 75%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since we are about four weeks away to the end of the circuit breaker measures, I wonder whether there is any step to mandate or at least offer this on an opt-out basis so that there will be a higher take-up rate and we will be able to leverage on technology to conduct aggressive tracing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, Apple and Google themselves have come out to talk about putting out a protocol that will be more effective when such apps are in place on their phones.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the technical teams are working very closely with Apple and Google to enhance the effectiveness of the app.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When that is done, we will certainly look at the next step, which is to see how the take-up rate of the app can be a lot more than what it is today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have one clarification for the Minister for Health and one for the Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Health, regarding his answer to what metrics the Government is using to decide whether to loosen the circuit breaker measures, he gave quite a comprehensive answer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But he did not mention this recognised indicator used by other countries called the effective reproduction number (or RE) of the virus in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister for Health whether our Government is actually tracking the RE of the virus in Singapore and if he could make that known and, if it is not, then why is the Government not using that indicator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Manpower, she touched earlier on the viral outbreak in the dormitories and how it might have been spread through contact, such as within dormitories and also at the construction sites.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, could it be linked to the workers returning from China?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Speaker, I want to thank Ms Sylvia Lim for the question on the reproductive number.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are, indeed, tracking the number very closely.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But as I have said, the numbers are important, but they are not everything.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, the reproductive number will be affected by the safe distancing and the circuit breaker measures that we have put in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The stricter the measures we put in place, in fact, we are suppressing the reproductive number.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, the risk, of course, is that once you remove the circuit breaker measures, the reproductive number may go up again because this basically measures how many persons you are likely to infect for a particular infected person.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, if you have very tight safe distancing and circuit breaker measures, even if you are infected, you do not have a chance to interact with other people and, therefore, you are not likely to infect more people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But once you remove these circuit breaker measures, you have more interaction and the risk of you transmitting the infection to other people will go up and, therefore, the reproductive number will go up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that we watch and monitor.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Of course, if you still have very high reproductive numbers, it is very difficult for you to liberalise your circuit breaker measures because it will just go up even further.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But even if you have very low reproductive numbers, you have to be very careful in opening up because, as you open up, the reproductive number may go up as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is something that we monitor and watch very carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the moment, I think the reproductive number in the community is significantly lower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is also reflected in the total number of cases that you see.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But in cases like the Safra outbreak, for example, you would expect the reproductive number to be significantly higher during that period of time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you look at the current infection in the dormitories, the reproductive numbers in the domitories are also likely to be higher.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, therefore, you need to look at the number quite carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, I would prefer not to produce one single number and try to peg our metrics on that number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Now, granted, in order to prevent a recurrence, we have to study and understand more deeply how it occurred in the first place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we may not have that luxury of a full understanding and still have to make adjustments in the best possible way based on whatever scientific knowledge and understanding we can muster at this point in time and applying the best of the technology and resources that we have available to us.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: My questions are for the Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In her Facebook post, the Minister said that each time the MOM attempts to raise the standard of living in these dormitories, it would face objections from employers due to the added costs that come with the move.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: My first question is: under the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act, the licenced operator and dormitory owner should be the parties to be held accountable to raise the standard of living in the dormitories in the interest of public health and safety.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, what did MOM involve the employer in the application of the provisions of this Act in this instance?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Any intention of the dormitory operator and owner to pass down the cost should be a separate matter for the parties to resolve later as the attempt by MOM to raise the living standard in the dormitories is done in the interest of public health and safety.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: My second question is: under the Act, operators must develop a quarantine plan in the event of an infectious disease outbreak.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Since the onset of the outbreak, taxpayers have been footing the bill for the quarantine exercise at these affected dormitories.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As this is a pandemic, would these dormitory operators and owners be held accountable for a share of the containment and quarantine costs?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Every month, the employers pay a certain sum to the dormitory operators to accommodate their workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Usually, the rooms are rented by one single employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, in any particular dormitory, you may have 400 or 500 rooms, whatever the number may be, and one employer takes one room.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within that room, depending on the size of that room, size of that unit, a certain number can be accommodated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, if as a result of a change in standards where we say that instead of accommodating X persons in one unit, eventually, they can only accommodate X-2 or X-3 persons per unit, then the cost per employee accommodated naturally goes up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Certainly, to the employer, this is something that they have to bear.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And whatever the business the employer is in, this goes into his cost considerations and, ultimately, he will pass it on to whoever buys his products and services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is something that we must always keep in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not so difficult for MOM, by the stroke of a pen, to change some numbers here and there.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we have to consider the overall implications and whether it is bearable for the employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the Member's second question on whether the costs eventually have to be apportioned, I think, the scale of COVID-19's impact on businesses and, certainly, even in the dormitories, it is just unprecedented.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At this point in time, if we were to start calculating the costs, I think it is very hard to move things; it is impossible to get things done.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Right now, the priority must be to keep the situation under control, bring it under control, and then, at the appropriate time, we can look at what are the right considerations in terms of handling the issue of costs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Just now, the Minister did not answer any of my four questions when I asked them in Chinese.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Now, I would like to ask them again in English.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Perhaps, there is no need to repeat them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Does the Minister need the questions to be repeated?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Does the Minister need me to ask in English or he will answer them?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, let me just state that the TCMs play an important part in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is complementary to our western medicine and we do want to allow them to continue to operate in a safe and managed way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we have always been allowing these TCM practices to continue, particularly through teleconsult, and for helping to look after the chronic patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But as I have said, as soon as the task force announced lifting some of the circuit breaker measures, we have a list of appeals from quite a lot of people all wanting to be part of the liberalisation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I can understand the anxiety of everybody because we have been on this circuit breaker for about a month, and tighter circuit breaker measures for about two weeks and I think everyone wants to see whether we can go back to normal.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I must share with you that we have very heated debates within the task force to decide what to liberalise and what not to liberalise.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the top of our concerns is to make sure that infection remains under control, the reproductive number remains low.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, it is important for us to do it in a calibrated way, in a managed way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I know there is still a lot of interest to open it up and we will continue to do so and we will be happy to get the task force to look at where else we could do so in a safe way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For the TCM practitioners, we consult them, we get their views and we also want to share with them our plans going forward.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I would assure Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that we will continue to engage them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the appropriate time, when we are more confident, and having done this first step of opening, if all goes well, we hope to be able to liberalise further.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Is it the same question from before or is it a new one?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: It is my third question that was not answered.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: A lot of my residents have requested to go to TCM shops to buy medicine to "bu tong" to build up their immune system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: So, can this be considered as one of the priorities?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: If you are allowing dessert shops to open on 12 May, I am sure TCM shops can also observe safe distancing, wearing of masks and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Basically, this is starting from the point of view that these TCM halls have to be opened.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When the TCM practitioners are seeing patients and they cannot give them the medicine, then how are the patients going to be treated?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we allow the medical halls to be opened if the TCM is seeing a patient.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even your residents can go to these halls to purchase their medication and we will look at how else we can expand this further.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 6.00 pm until 6.20 pm.
